The rhaita or ghaita (Arabic: غيطة, romanised: ghayṭa) is a double-reed instrument from north-west Africa, found in Morocco, Algeria, Libya and Mauritania and occasionally in Tunisia. Its construction is almost exactly that of the Arabic mizmar and the Turkish zurna. Its distinctive name comes from a medieval Gothic-Iberian influence. In southern Iberia various wind instruments, including the related shawm, are called gaitas, but in northern Iberia gaita refers only to bagpipes.
萊塔管源於西北非洲的摩洛哥、阿爾及利亞、利比亞和茅利塔尼亞等地區。作為一種雙簧管: The rhaita comes from Morocco, Algeria, Libya and Mauritania and neighbouring parts of north-west Africa. As a double-reed instrument its construction is very close to the Arabic mizmar and the Turkish zurna, which reflects the wide links between the instrument cultures of the Middle East and North Africa. Its distinctive naming comes from the cultural influence of the medieval Iberian peninsula, and especially from the deep traces left by Muslim rule. In southern Iberia gaitas once meant all sorts of wind instruments and the related shawms; in northern Iberia gaita means only bagpipes. The development of the rhaita shows where Islamic civilisation and Iberian culture met, and the lines along which it spread make plain how instrument cultures of the Mediterranean influenced and merged with one another; to this day it holds an important place in the folk music of North Africa.

The listening occasions the sources mention are mainly modern composition and film music: Howard Shore uses its timbre in the Mordor theme of The Lord of the Rings soundtrack; John Corigliano, in the 'Rhaita Dance' of his 1975 Concerto for Oboe and Orchestra, asks the oboist to push the reed further into the mouth to imitate the rhaita; and in 'Three Hallucinations' from the 1981 Altered States soundtrack the oboe is again asked to imitate its sound.
萊塔管音色高亢明亮，具有穿透力強的特徵，能在戶外廣場與慶典中遠距離傳播。其音質帶: The rhaita's timbre is high and bright, with great carrying power, so it travels far across an outdoor square or a celebration. The quality has something rough in it, rich in North African character, and the range sits mainly in the upper middle and high register. The instrument resonates through the vibration of the double reed, which makes the sound both exciting and tough. Next to the warm softness of the Arabic mizmar, the rhaita's quality is sharper and rougher; next to the Turkish zurna its timbre is a little more piercing, yet in folk ritual it is just as recognisable. Its whole sound is full of raw force, often used at weddings, festivals and military events, where it can build a heated, jubilant atmosphere.
